findings.text: Within one paragraph, a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. The page's first job is done well.
findings.source: header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next step is linked near the top, and the install path is concrete: prerequisites, clone, setup and a first command. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section with `git clone`, `./setup.sh`, `athena ask "add a changelog"`

findings.text: This page is served at Athena's own address, yet almost all of it is a detailed state-machine study of a different tool, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena has to scroll past dozens of cards and 45 claims that are of no use for deciding whether to try Athena.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections States, Counters, Transitions, Claims and sources

findings.text: The page describes two products, commits made from requests and studies of other projects, but never says how they relate. It shows no example of the main product (a traced commit), and the Next steps do not say how to produce a study like this one.
findings.source: lede: "turns a short request into a change to a code repository" vs. "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project"

findings.text: A newcomer can tell that Athena runs paid AI models but is not told whether they need an account or API key, or roughly what a run costs. These are likely the first questions before trying it.
findings.source: Next steps: "either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)" and lede "records what each step cost"

findings.text: The page does not say which repository the command acts on (presumably the current directory) or whether Athena commits right away. A cautious newcomer would want to know both before pressing Enter.
findings.source: Next steps: "press Enter to run it on your repository"

findings.text: This link sits next to the newcomer's next step but is meant for the project owner. To a stranger, "your decision" is confusing.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: This refers to internal repository layout that a newcomer cannot see or use.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"

findings.text: The firstmate study itself is careful for a reader who does want it: terms are defined before use, every statement links to source lines, and gaps are stated honestly ("this page gives no test for it", "No bound on relaunches was found").
findings.source: Start here / Words used first and the Glossary

findings.text: Each state line gives only a name and a tag, with no description. The reader has to go to the Glossary to learn what, for example, "ready" or "close-pending" means.
findings.source: States of a piece of work: "Read each line as the state's name, its kind, and the claims that support it."
